improvement_notes: Replace the sentence “An illustrator should show...” with direct learner-facing guidance, since the visual has already been generated and published.

The lesson is exceptionally thorough for an introductory class, but several feedback terminology caveats recur. Consolidate the distinctions between feedback, sensor-triggered action, and sustained feedback regulation into one concise explanation and reuse a shorter reference later.

Add an explicit worked trace for the two-speed challenge, or provide a compact table showing the measured distance, error, selected speed, and resulting true distance. The self-check is correct but requires students to reconstruct the computation themselves.

Clarify that the proportional equation v = ke is valid here only for positive approach error and requires a sign convention, directional convention, and output limit in a complete controller. As written, a beginner could incorrectly apply it to negative error or command reverse motion without qualification.

The code records state after the action but records the measurement before the action. State this explicitly in the table explanation so learners do not confuse the measurement used for a decision with the resulting post-action distance.

Consider adding a brief note that a real distance sensor may measure along a beam or field of view rather than the rover's exact perpendicular distance to a wall. This would strengthen the calibration and model-assumption discussion without adding much complexity.

The visual plan is relevant and coherent, but four similar generated diagrams may create visual redundancy. Ensure each figure has a distinct instructional job and consider removing or replacing one if the rendered layouts repeat the same block-loop idea.

Add a short accessibility note for the diagrams, such as identifying arrows by labels and direction rather than color alone. The existing alt text is strong but could mention the key decision threshold where appropriate.

A real hardware photograph would materially improve grounding, particularly in the Real Robot Connection section, provided it is independently licensed and clearly distinguished from the generated diagrams.

linkedin.title: Sense → Think → Act: Teaching Feedback Control Through RoboRover
linkedin.description: A practical robotics lesson that connects sensors, controllers, actuators, error equations, noisy measurements, and Python simulation through a safety-conscious RoboRover lab.
linkedin.commentary:
A strong robotics foundation begins with a clear question: how does information become motion?

This Professor OS lesson uses RoboRover to make the sense → think → act loop concrete:

• Sensors turn physical conditions into measurements.
• Controllers use goals and measurements to select commands.
• Actuators turn commands into physical effects.
• Feedback connects the changed world back to the next decision.
• A Python simulation lets students test noise, tolerance, overshoot, and speed safely.

The lesson also distinguishes a simple threshold controller from proportional control, introduces units and control error, and makes the limits of simulation explicit. That combination helps beginners build correct mental models before working with physical hardware.

Try the lab: predict how many forward commands RoboRover will issue, run the simulation, then change one parameter and explain the result.
